learningPath.name: Understand
learningPath.description: Recognize the components of a financial return and the intuition behind each term.

learningPath.name: Calculate
learningPath.description: Compute one-period price, income and total returns reliably.

learningPath.name: Chain
learningPath.description: Combine returns across periods using wealth relatives rather than arithmetic addition.

learningPath.name: Annualize
learningPath.description: Convert cumulative multi-period performance into an annual compound rate.

learningPath.name: Reverse solve
learningPath.description: Solve for a missing price, distribution or return from the return identity.

learningPath.name: Master
learningPath.description: Pass mixed, timed and confidence-calibrated questions without fragile guesses.

concepts.name: Holding-Period Return
concepts.summary: Measures total gain or loss over one holding period relative to the initial investment.
concepts.intuition: Start with what you paid, add what you received, compare with what you ended with.
traps: Dividing by ending value instead of beginning value

concepts.name: Price Return
concepts.summary: The capital gain or loss component generated only by the change in asset price.
concepts.intuition: Ignore cash income and ask how much the market price itself changed relative to the starting price.

concepts.name: Income Yield
concepts.summary: The cash distribution received during the holding period relative to the initial investment.
concepts.intuition: Income is a separate return engine from the change in market price.
traps: Confusing income yield with total return

concepts.name: Total-Return Decomposition
concepts.summary: For a one-period asset return, total return is the price-return component plus the income-yield component.
concepts.intuition: Every unit of performance must come from price movement, cash income, or both.
traps: Adding percentages built on different denominators

concepts.name: Wealth Relative
concepts.summary: The factor 1 + R converts a return into a multiplicative growth factor.
concepts.intuition: Returns compound by multiplying growth factors, not by repeatedly adding percentages.

concepts.name: Multi-Period Cumulative Return
concepts.summary: Combines sequential returns by multiplying wealth relatives and subtracting one.
concepts.intuition: Each period acts on the wealth left by the previous period.
traps: Forgetting to subtract one after multiplying factors

concepts.name: Annualized Compound Return
concepts.summary: The constant annual compound rate that reproduces a multi-year cumulative return.
concepts.intuition: Find the equal yearly growth factor whose repeated multiplication reaches the same terminal wealth.
traps: Dividing cumulative return by the number of years
Using n instead of 1/n as the exponent

concepts.name: Reverse Return Problems
concepts.summary: Rearranges the return identity to solve for an unknown beginning price, ending price, income or required return.
concepts.intuition: The same return equation should work in both directions; do not memorize separate formulas unnecessarily.
traps: Applying the return to the ending rather than beginning value

formulas.name: Holding-Period Return
formulas.explanation: Total one-period return combines the capital gain/loss and cash income, divided by beginning value.

formulas.name: Ending Value from Required Return
formulas.explanation: Rearrangement of the holding-period return identity.

flashcards.front: What belongs in a one-period total return?
flashcards.back: Price change plus cash distributions, all relative to beginning value.

flashcards.front: What denominator anchors a standard holding-period return?
flashcards.back: The beginning price or beginning invested value.

flashcards.front: Does a dividend belong in price return?
flashcards.back: No. Price return isolates the change in market price.

flashcards.front: How do you express cash income as a return component?
flashcards.back: Cash distribution divided by beginning value.

flashcards.front: One-period total return decomposes into which two components?
A return of -20% corresponds to what wealth relative?

flashcards.back: They apply to different wealth bases: 1.20 × 0.80 = 0.96, a 4% loss.

flashcards.front: How do you combine sequential period returns?
flashcards.back: Multiply their wealth relatives and subtract one.

flashcards.front: When is adding period returns generally wrong?
flashcards.back: When measuring compounded multi-period performance rather than an approximation for very small returns.

flashcards.front: Why is cumulative return / years usually not the annual compound return?
flashcards.back: Because compounding is multiplicative; annualization uses the nth root of the cumulative wealth factor.

flashcards.front: What does an annualized compound return represent?
flashcards.back: The constant annual rate that would produce the same terminal wealth over n years.

flashcards.front: If required return and distribution are known, how do you solve for ending price?
flashcards.back: Rearrange the holding-period return identity: ending value = beginning value × (1 + return) − distribution.
